I am not a parent but I remember what my parents did.

They raised us on healthy food, firstly. Sure we had cookies and chocolate milk sometimes, but those were treats. And treats were ok. We weren't scared of having treats because we had them rarely enough that there was no reason to be worried about their existence in our lives. We rarely had McDonalds, usually it would be a special treat coupled with a rented video on the first night dad left for hunting trips. But a typical snack was sliced apple with cinnamon sprinkled on it. Or bananas. Crackers with cheese. If we were at the store buying groceries mum would ask "What kind of healthy snacks would you like for school?" That question never brought up the option for junk food, so junk food was not the focus. We would come up with fruit we liked, or those mini peanut butter bread stick dip things (not super good for you but they weren't gushers and dunkaroos giving childhood beetus). If I saw a commercial on TV for shitty candy cereal like the kind with marshmallows and technicolor "cereal" pieces and asked for it, my parents would explain that it has too much sugar which could make a person very sick if they ate too much. So we'd get apple cinnamon cheerios or something else that was tasty but less shitty.

Healthy food was also fun for us. We used to LOVE the movie Land Before Time, and as kids decided that broccoli looked exactly like "green food!!!" so we'd happily much on it pretending to be dinosaurs. We'd specifically ask mum to buy broccoli at the store (she was very proud) and I'd ask for "white broccoli" because I could never remember how to say cauliflower.

We were always put into soccer or dance, went on family hikes and bike rides. We all kept very active and I know that part of this was a lack of technology in our house. We didn't have a family computer until I was maybe 10, and no matter how much I asked for a gameboy+pokemon my parents decided that I'd probably sit around all day being lazy if I had one and never obliged. I am grateful for that now. We live beside a forest and there's a big pond behind my house, during the summer I would invite friends over to catch frogs. Being outside was fun. Kids these days aren't allowed to get dirty and they're handed tablets by the age of 4 so parents can ignore them. Don't give your kids technology too early in life, it leads to laziness.

And lastly, there were the occasional comments coming from somewhere about other people's weight. It was usually said in a mocking way by a visiting grandfather (everyone has one of those offensive grandparents...) to which mum would quietly say to us that he was no one to talk, having a good amount of girth himself. We'd giggle. This would teach us that fat = humiliating. Or it would be in a very sad way, my mum has a beautiful heart and not a mean bone in her body, so when TLC special came on about people too fat to get off their couches she'd say "I can't imagine not being able to put my arms down with all those rolls in the way, it looks so uncomfortable. It must feel awful to never be able to go outside without being laughed at." This would teach us that fat = depressed. Or dad would see some fatty on tv or downtown and point them out to us and say, "Look at that big fat guy. He probably has a hard time doing things like walking upstairs. Mommy and I try to make sure you guys eat good food and go outside to play, so you don't end up like that guy." This taught us that fat = bad habits, and a choice you make.

There were never numbers on a scale. There were never comments about our bodies. We never learned the word calorie. We were just raised with healthy habits and a gentle forewarning about what neglecting healthy habits can do. Since we were never fat or unhealthy, "fat" was the "other." It had nothing to do with us. We didn't have to worry about being fat.

It wasn't just fat, either. Dad would watch intervention shows and warn us about drugs. Or prison shows and warn us about behaviour. We learned kindness by helping wild animals we came across with mum (we named a lost robin Robin, 10/10 creativity points) and we learned charity by donating old toys we never played with. We were well rounded, never focused on one aspect of our lives enough for it to take over our minds.

If you are a healthy parent, behave healthy in front of your kids, raise them with healthy habits, and once in a while mention that healthy habits are important and neglecting them can be harmful, then you will have no problem with your kids. Raise them with the idea that healthy is normal, not that fatness is evil. They will learn that part as they get older, but as kids it should be a non-issue for them. Telling your child there are calories in their food that will make them fat will make them afraid of food. Telling your kid they will get fat if they eat those cookies will make them feel guilty for having them. So it is important to raise them with the idea that health is the standard so much so that it doesn't need to be focused on.

Remember to treat yours kids, too. Avoiding every sweet thing int he world will only make them want to indulge. Teaching them that it is ok to have and ice cream cone on a hot summer day will help ensure that their healthy habits wont turn into an unhealthy obsession.

This is long, but if any of it helps then it's worth it.

We were always put into soccer or dance, went on family hikes and bike rides. We all kept very active and I know that part of this was a lack of technology in our house. We didn't have a family computer until I was maybe 10, and no matter how much I asked for a gameboy+pokemon my parents decided that I'd probably sit around all day being lazy if I had one and never obliged. I am grateful for that now. We live beside a forest and there's a big pond behind my house, during the summer I would invite friends over to catch frogs. Being outside was fun. Kids these days aren't allowed to get dirty and they're handed tablets by the age of 4 so parents can ignore them. Don't give your kids technology too early in life, it leads to laziness.

And lastly, there were the occasional comments coming from somewhere about other people's weight. It was usually said in a mocking way by a visiting grandfather (everyone has one of those offensive grandparents...) to which mum would quietly say to us that he was no one to talk, having a good amount of girth himself. We'd giggle. This would teach us that fat = humiliating. Or it would be in a very sad way, my mum has a beautiful heart and not a mean bone in her body, so when TLC special came on about people too fat to get off their couches she'd say "I can't imagine not being able to put my arms down with all those rolls in the way, it looks so uncomfortable. It must feel awful to never be able to go outside without being laughed at." This would teach us that fat = depressed. Or dad would see some fatty on tv or downtown and point them out to us and say, "Look at that big fat guy. He probably has a hard time doing things like walking upstairs. Mommy and I try to make sure you guys eat good food and go outside to play, so you don't end up like that guy." This taught us that fat = bad habits, and a choice you make.

There were never numbers on a scale. There were never comments about our bodies. We never learned the word calorie. We were just raised with healthy habits and a gentle forewarning about what neglecting healthy habits can do. Since we were never fat or unhealthy, "fat" was the "other." It had nothing to do with us. We didn't have to worry about being fat.

It wasn't just fat, either. Dad would watch intervention shows and warn us about drugs. Or prison shows and warn us about behaviour. We learned kindness by helping wild animals we came across with mum (we named a lost robin Robin, 10/10 creativity points) and we learned charity by donating old toys we never played with. We were well rounded, never focused on one aspect of our lives enough for it to take over our minds.

If you are a healthy parent, behave healthy in front of your kids, raise them with healthy habits, and once in a while mention that healthy habits are important and neglecting them can be harmful, then you will have no problem with your kids. Raise them with the idea that healthy is normal, not that fatness is evil. They will learn that part as they get older, but as kids it should be a non-issue for them. Telling your child there are calories in their food that will make them fat will make them afraid of food. Telling your kid they will get fat if they eat those cookies will make them feel guilty for having them. So it is important to raise them with the idea that health is the standard so much so that it doesn't need to be focused on.

Remember to treat yours kids, too. Avoiding every sweet thing int he world will only make them want to indulge. Teaching them that it is ok to have and ice cream cone on a hot summer day will help ensure that their healthy habits wont turn into an unhealthy obsession.

This is long, but if any of it helps then it's worth it.

I really like "French Kids Eat Everything" as a primer for fostering a healthy food culture in the home. I'm sure it's easier if the culture beyond your doorstep isn't actively trying to shove trash into your children's mouths, but we do OK.

With my toddler, we eat the same foods pretty much every meal. I'm pregnant with my second now too, so I've really been watching what I eat. He doesn't talk much yet, but he's always asking for apples or nanas whenever he wakes up. I always keep fruit around the house for snack time and breakfast, so he incorporates fruit being a snack. He also really loves raw or steamed veggies, hopefully it stays that way! I'm also a vegetarian, so that's helped keep it on track with fresh foods. His dad eats meat though, and that kid will demolish meats, especially steak or chicken.

I try to keep him away from processed foods as much as possible, although I'm really trying not to be too overbearing. He has sugar once in a while, but being so young I don't want him craving it all the time. We're obviously still at the point of him not being able to grab any food by himself yet, so it hasn't been too bad. Like everyone else has said, pretty much lead by example. He's one of the only kids his age I ever really see drink water too.

Not an actual parent, but I take a lot of responsibility for baby bro because reasons.

When he asks me for sweets I usually tell him no. If he asks why I tell him it's bad for him. If he continues asking (ugh, kids always do) I start a conversation about teeth and bodies, and about sugar only being good in small amounts. That junk food doesn't contain anything he needs. When he talks about wanting to build muscle when he gets older I tell him he needs to eat protein for that, and in which food he can find it.

He's a real twig though. Picky eater. He would benefit from gaining a little, but from real food and not from candy. He's picky with sweets too and that's probably good. Wouldn't want a fat brother.
